observations: Native acceptance ran as a non-root user in a freshly provisioned Ubuntu 24.04 container on Linux arm64 with Codex 0.155.1 and its Linux sandbox active, against the frozen commit copied into a writable checkout, with a throwaway home, Codex home and Claude configuration directory per probe.

Installation produced 59 links, a 16,250-byte Codex AGENTS file, 11 role definitions, 20 skills and the harness-owned project fallback key; the client's own prompt render showed 37,149 characters carrying the harness instructions, every resolved stance, the identity block and the harness skill root.

A second sync left the generated file byte-identical with a clean diff and a doctor run reporting no drift and naming absent tools as not on PATH, and appending a line to a managed file made the diff report a modified generated file and exit 1 with the next sync exiting 2.

Switching the voice, commits and delegation stances changed both the client's prompt render and its behaviour: the same probe moved from a Conventional Commits subject to a plain sentence and from a sizing judgement about delegating to a flat statement that subagents are prohibited, and an unknown variant was refused by name with its options listed.

A custom dimension from a private primitive root resolved to its external file and changed native replies from TAGGED to PLAIN when the selected variant changed, while a session variable, a project stances file reached through its environment variable and an invalid choice all resolved through the same primitive authority, and a project file carrying identity was refused.

A stance selected only through a HARNESS_STANCE session variable was resolved by the stances command but was not linked by a sync run under the same variable, which exited 0 and left the previous variant in the client's instructions with a clean diff.

Manual mode refused a native write with the client's own read-only sandbox rejection and no file appeared, auto and explicitly acknowledged bypass created their sentinels, and bypass without acknowledgement failed the sync and left the prior state reported by the client.

The client's own configuration introspection reported the approvals reviewer as user under manual and auto review under auto with the older key absent in every posture, and doctor named the client version and the key it accepts.

Registered hooks stayed inert until hook trust was satisfied, after which a separate user hook composed with the harness hook on the same events, a grade-3 command was blocked by the client with the harness reason, and one multi-file patch drew independent Review Card feedback for both plan files, quoted back verbatim.

On this commit an allowed call reports no hook failure: an applied patch and a read-only shell command each showed the composed pre-tool hooks completing twice with no failed hook line, which is the shape that produced an unexplained failure on the previous freeze.

Isolated gatherer and planner workers completed under native read restrictions with result authority limited to data and no transferred approval; their workspace and out-of-scope writes never appeared, and planner publication into the approved plans slot stayed harness-mediated and carried the Review Card headings.

Both real workers recorded the new process identity and start-time fields in their worker state, and a worker whose recorded process no longer exists and reported no result was read back as orphaned with a stderr line saying so, from a fixture rather than a killed process.

Selecting the frugal cost variant rewrote exactly five of the eleven Codex role definitions and left the other six byte-identical, and the isolated worker resolved the same row the sync rendered, moving the gatherer to the standard class while the fixed reviewer kept its own class, effort and budget sentence.

A completed worker's posture block recorded the selected variant, the resolved class and the cost-row source of class and effort with the row's budget figures; the usage feed is not applicable because this runtime raises none of the feed's events.

The stop gate ran once on a trusted repository and recorded a green result, reused it on an unchanged tree, reran for an untracked file and for a staged edit, and blocked the turn while the gate was red without recording a green result until the failure was repaired.

One task was carried natively across both directions, advancing revisions 1, 2 and 3 with the writing runtime recorded each time, turning stale with an unverified verification after the tree changed and current again when it was reverted, and transferring no approval.
A save at an already-used revision was refused with exit 1 and a single stderr line naming the remedy, with no traceback and no absolute path, which is the presentation the previous freeze got wrong.

Migration and uninstall preserved user data: an unadopted file was refused, adoption merged only the owned key, a hand-changed owned key and a replaced managed link were reported rather than overwritten, and uninstall restored the adopted file byte-for-byte while leaving unrelated settings and session files untouched.
Uninstall left no harness stance rules directory and no harness skill entries behind, removing each projection by name rather than leaving empty shells.

The pinned BMad runtime installed cleanly into a disposable framework checkout, the harness check reported no drift, apply installed the three workflow templates, and resolving the review customization with that checkout as project root yielded four layers whose instructions all route through an isolated role worker.

A code review of a nine-line seeded diff in an assigned worktree ran from the framework checkout with three review layers launched as isolated workers, each writing worker state and completing with a result; the fourth layer was skipped by the recipe's own no-spec condition rather than by a routing loss.

The triaged report named both seeded defects, routing the discount unit error to patch on two layers' agreement and rejecting the empty-input division with a stated reason, and reported no failed layers.
